newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. urges study of "mass destruction" terrorism.
newsitem.headline: U.N. urges study of "mass destruction" terrorism.

text.p: The United Nations should consider how to combat terrorism involving the use of weapons of mass destruction and the disruption of communications networks, a U.N. report said on Wednesday.

The report was requested by a December 1995 General Assembly resolution that asked Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali to analyse existing anti-terrorism measures "to assist states in identifying aspects of this matter that have not been covered by such (legal) instruments."
The report said most of 13 existing anti-terrorism agreements were introduced "after significant international incidents had already taken place."

They dealt with such things as terrorism against civil aviation and maritime activities, including hijacking and attacks against aircraft, shipping and airports. They also covered attacks against government leaders and diplomats, hostage-taking and the marking of plastic explosives to make them detectable.

"There seems to be a point to consider the need to promulgate international treaties or other kinds of instruments in areas or with respect to subjects which are not covered by existing treaties," the report suggested.

"Consideration may be given to: terrorist bombings, terrorist fund-raising, traffic in arms, money laundering, exchange of information concerning persons or organisations suspected of terrorist-linked activities, falsification of travel documents, technical cooperation in training for counter-terrorism, and so forth."

The report continued: "Attention should also be given to preventing the use of weapons of mass destruction by terrorists and the use of modern information technology for terrorist purposes, such as disrupting a communications network by altering data or disseminating on a wide scale extremist ideologies inciting persons to commit terrorist acts."
